> I'm actually giving it a crack now, but seem to be getting an error,

> or how to resolve....
>

> /Error in chol.default(S) : /
> / the leading minor of order 55 is not positive definite/
> /Error in lavSampleStatsFromData(Data = lavaanData, rescale =
> (lavaanOptions$estimator == : /
> / lavaan ERROR: sample covariance can not be inverted/

The sample covariance matrix (S) of the observed variables in your data
is not positive-definite (ie not of full rank). Therefore, it can not be
inverted.

Perhaps some of the predictors can be written as a linear combination of
others? You need to get rid of these redundant predictors first, to get
an 'X' matrix which is of full rank.

Before you do your analysis, you can use

qr(X)$rank

to check the rank of the matrix X.

Yves.

On 10/23/2012 03:36 PM, Nicholas Hamilton wrote:
> Is there really a point to modelling data, if that very model cannot be
> used for processing new data?.... ;-)

SEM is not about prediction. It is about model fit. Once you have a good
'working' model, and you have new data, you just fit the model again
using the new data. If the model fits well (again), you have additional
evidence in favor of your model. This is the SEM paradigm.

Yves.

messages.author: 253141a6efac547e
messages.subject: Re: Basic Question
parts:
Alternately, if it is a recursive SEM with only observed variables, you should be able to take simulated draws of the coefficients and errors to get predictions with 95% CIs on them. It will just take some doing on your part.

Here's a simple example - although it does make me wonder if, for a case like this, this could be automated…

Sorry, haven't dug into lavaan's guts lately to come up with a classier more elegant solution for this one.

library(lavaan)

#create a data frame
set.seed(1001)
n <- 100
adf <- data.frame(x1 = rnorm(n))
adf <- within(adf, {
x2 <- rnorm(n)
y1 <- rnorm(n, x1 + x2)
y2 <- rnorm(n, y1 + x2)
})

#create a fit sem object
model <- '
y1 ~ x1 + x2
y2 ~ y1 + x2
'
fit <- sem(model, data = adf)



#now, use simulation to determine
#a new y2 value based on x1 and x2
n.sims <- 100
new.x <- c(1,2)

#get the coefficients
coefs <- rmvnorm(n.sims, coef(fit), vcov(fit))

#get the residual SE for each response variable
#using the inverse chisq distribution
df <- nrow(adf)-1
X <- matrix(rchisq(n.sims*2, df=df), ncol=2)
ses <- sqrt( coef(fit)[5:6]) * sqrt(df/X)

#calculate the new y1 and y3
y1.pred <- rnorm(100, coefs[,1]*new.x[1] + coefs[,2] *new.x[2],ses[1])
y2.pred <- rnorm(100, coefs[,3]*y1.pred + coefs[,4] *new.x[2], ses[2])

#get some properties
mean(y2.pred)
sd(y2.pred)

Taking it back to grass roots level, lets say a model is trained, y ~
x, against two data points on the x/y plane, representing (0,0) and
(1,1). Obviously this would result in a model describing the formula
y = mx + b, where m = 1 and b = 0. I should be able to put in a
vector of values for x, (with unknown y), to return another vector of
values representing y, so if I put in x = [0.5, 1.5, 3] one would
expect it to return y = [0.5, 1.5, 3] which satisfies the originally
fitted model without any further training / fitting.

Sure. The simple regression case is easy. But you don't need lavaan for that. The general SEM case. Not so easy. Again, show me the literature, and I will implement it.

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: Basic Question
parts:
At the beginning of this thread, I suggested to use predict(), with a
newdata argument. Unfortunately, it turned out that the newdata argument
for the predict() function in lavaan was not even implemented. An
oversight on my part, which is now fixed, and the dev version (0.5-10)
now has a newdata argument. You can install the dev version by typing in R:

install.packages("lavaan", repos="http://www.da.ugent.be", type="source")

I also mentioned a couple of times that the predict() function in lavaan
only produces factor scores. Hence, for observed-variables-only models,
this is not very useful. On the other hand, you can always create
phantom latent variables (with a single indicator). In this case, all
the regressions are among latent variables. And, you can use predict()
to get (factor) scores.

In other words, to get your predictions, simply 'upgrade' the dependent
variables to latent variables with a single indicator, and use the
predict() function with new data.

An artificial example:

myModel <- ' # path model
x1 ~ x2 + x3
x3 ~ x4 + x5
x5 ~ x6 + x8

# upgrading endogenous variables to latents
fx1 =~ x1
fx3 =~ x3
fx5 =~ x5
'

fit <- sem(model=myModel, data=HolzingerSwineford1939)
predict(fit)

# create new dataset - should contain the same variable names as original
HS20 <- HolzingerSwineford1939[1:20,]

predict(fit, newdata=HS20)


Yves.
